notes.meaning: Peter now quotes Psalm 16 to show that the Messiah, God's promised King, had to rise from the dead. In it David says he kept the Lord always in view and trusted Him as a helper standing right beside him. Because God was at his side, nothing could knock him down. Peter reads these words as speaking about Jesus.

differ.view: David was describing his own trust in God, and his experience was a picture of the Messiah's.
The psalm speaks of the Messiah alone. Making it mainly about David weakens Peter's whole argument.

notes.meaning: Because God was near, the speaker's heart was glad and his mouth praised God. Even his body could rest in the grave 'in hope,' sure that it would be raised. Peter sees here Jesus facing death calmly, trusting the Father to raise Him. Christians can be laid in the grave with that same hope.

'Hades' here means the world of the dead, not the place of punishment. God would not leave His 'Holy One,' the one set apart for Him, among the dead. Nor would He let that body rot in the grave. Jesus truly died, but He was raised before His body could decay.

'The paths of life' means the way back to life: God would raise Him from the dead. 'Joy in Your presence' points to the gladness of being welcomed by the Father when Jesus went up to heaven. Instead of being left in death, He was rewarded.

Peter speaks to them warmly as 'brothers.' He reminds them that David, the honored founder of Israel's royal family, died and was buried. His tomb was still there in Jerusalem for anyone to see. No one ever claimed David rose, so the psalm could not be about him.

But David was also a prophet, someone God gave messages about the future. God had made him a solemn promise, sealed with an oath, that one of his descendants would rule on his throne (2 Samuel 7; Psalm 132). David knew this coming King would be the Messiah.

Looking ahead, David saw that this promised King would rise from the dead. So in Psalm 16 he was speaking of the Messiah's resurrection. David died before that kingdom came, and it was to last forever, so its King had to live again. He would not be left among the dead, and His body would not decay.
Peter now says plainly that God did this for Jesus. He and the other believers had seen Jesus alive after His death, and had talked and eaten with Him. So what David foretold had come true in Jesus.

After rising, Jesus was lifted up to the highest place of honor and power, at God's 'right hand.' From the Father He received the promised Holy Spirit, and He has poured the Spirit out. The sound, the flames and the many languages the crowd saw and heard were His doing. They proved that Jesus was alive and reigning.

David himself never went up into heaven as Jesus did. Yet in Psalm 110 David heard God speak to someone David called 'my Lord,' telling Him to sit at His right hand. Sitting there meant the highest honor and rule. Making enemies a 'footstool' pictures complete victory, as conquerors once put their feet on beaten foes.

Peter ends with his main point. The very Jesus they crucified is the one God has raised to be Lord, ruler of all, and Christ, the promised Messiah. 'Made' means God gave Him this rank and honor, not that He became God's Son at that moment. This showed their guilt clearly and called them to bow to Him.

The people felt a sharp pain in their hearts, as if stabbed. They saw that they had helped kill their own Messiah. Instead of mocking, they now called the apostles 'brothers' and begged to know what to do. Sorrow like this over sin is where turning to God begins.

Peter told them to repent, which means to change their mind and turn from sin to God. Each one was to be baptized (washed with water) in the name of Jesus, openly declaring Him their Savior and Lord. God promised them forgiveness of their sins and the gift of the Holy Spirit Himself.

differ.view: Forgiveness comes when a person repents and believes; baptism follows as a public sign. The word 'for' can mean 'because of,' and Peter's later sermons promise forgiveness without mentioning baptism.
Baptism is God's seal on the forgiveness received by faith. It confirms and strengthens faith but does not work automatically.
Baptism here goes with repenting, as the outward sign of faith, rather than being what brings forgiveness. Reading 'for' as 'because of' is possible but unlikely.
Baptism points to the Spirit's cleansing of the heart. The water itself does not clean the conscience, but those who use the sign faithfully receive what it points to.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Peter tells them to be baptized in order to receive forgiveness and the Spirit. This shows that baptism is needed for salvation.

notes.meaning: The promise is God's promise of forgiveness and the Holy Spirit, foretold by the prophet Joel. It is for these Jewish hearers, even though they crucified Jesus, and for their children after them. It also reaches 'those far off,' which came to mean people of every nation. Everyone God calls to Himself may share in it.

differ.view: 'Your children' includes the babies of believers. Just as children received circumcision in the old covenant, they should receive baptism now.
'You,' 'your children' and 'those far off' are all called the same way: to repent. So the verse is about descendants who respond in faith, not about baptizing infants.

notes.meaning: Luke gives only a summary; Peter said much more and kept pleading with them. He urged them to be saved from the twisted, stubborn people of that day who had rejected Jesus. That meant breaking away from their unbelief and the judgment coming on it. Following Christ means not going along with those who oppose Him.

Those who gladly accepted the message were baptized. About three thousand people joined the believers that day, added to the roughly 120 already there. They came freely and joyfully, not under pressure. It was the first great harvest of the Spirit's work through the gospel.

differ.view: It is hard to picture three thousand people being fully dipped under water in the city in one day, so some may have been baptized another way, perhaps by sprinkling.
Jerusalem's many pools and ritual baths gave plenty of water to baptize that many people by dipping them under.

notes.meaning: The new believers kept at four things. They listened closely to the apostles' teaching and shared their lives in fellowship. They broke bread together, which many understand as the Lord's Supper (Communion), and they prayed together. These four things picture what a true church looks like.

differ.view: 'Breaking of bread' may mean their ordinary shared meals, or meals followed by the Lord's Supper; we cannot be sure.

notes.meaning: A deep awe, a holy fear, came over the people of the city, not only the believers. The apostles did many miracles, which showed their message came from God. This awe also held back opposition so the young church could grow.

The believers were joined in heart and often met together. They treated what they owned as available to anyone in need. Some sold land, houses or goods and shared the money as needs came up. No one forced them; love moved them, and it did away with selfishness rather than with owning things.

differ.view: This sharing was the natural fruit of love, and there is no proof Christ meant it to stop. If the church had kept that love, the practice would have continued.
This was an unusual case for that time and place, never commanded and not done elsewhere, so it is not a rule for all Christians. It still teaches that those with plenty should help the poor.

notes.meaning: Every day the believers met together in the temple courts at the regular hours of prayer. They also broke bread in one another's homes. They ate their meals with glad, simple and sincere hearts, free from worry and showing off.

differ.view: Breaking bread at home included the Lord's Supper, which they shared daily.
Breaking bread here means ordinary shared meals at home, eaten with joy, not the Lord's Supper.

notes.meaning: They kept praising God, and most ordinary people thought well of them because of their kind, honest lives. Day after day the Lord Himself added people who were being saved. Growth in the church is God's work, not just human effort.

differ.view: Those added were the people God had chosen for salvation, and God surely brings every one of them to Christ.
'Being saved' means people who were then being saved from the guilt and power of their sins. It does not mean everyone added was sure to be saved forever no matter what.

problems: v. 39: dropped other point (Catholic): no checkable source
